passages.text: Non-Invasive Assessment of Microvascular Invasion Risk in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Using Liquid Biopsy: Translational Insights and Clinical Implications

Microvascular invasion (MVI) is a critical prognostic indicator for recurrence and survival in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, its accurate preoperative assessment remains clinically challenging. <sentence_start/>Postoperative histopathology is subject to sampling bias and time delays, while traditional imaging techniques lack the molecular specificity required to predict MVI. <sentence_start/>Liquid biopsy, through the analysis of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells (CTCs), circulating tumor RNA (ctRNA), and extracellular vesicles (EVs), provides a minimally invasive approach for capturing tumor-derived molecular and cellular signals associated with vascular invasion. <sentence_start/>This narrative review comprehensively summarizes the current evidence linking these four liquid biopsy analyte categories to MVI in HCC, evaluates their integration into multi-omics predictive models, including multi-marker, clinicopathological-integrated, and imaging-integrated strategies, and proposes an evidence-level framework that categorizes blood biomarkers according to the strength of their support for MVI prediction, distinguishing direct histopathological validation from indirect associations with aggressive tumor biology. <sentence_start/>Key challenges are critically examined, including the variable specificity of individual biomarkers for MVI, the lack of head-to-head comparative studies, the absence of standardized pre-analytical and analytical protocols, and the methodological limitations of current prediction models. <sentence_start/>As a narrative review, this work does not employ systematic review methodology, and the evidence synthesis should be interpreted accordingly. <sentence_start/>The review provides a framework for understanding how liquid biopsy-based MVI risk stratification may inform surgical and perioperative decision-making following prospective validation.
1. Introduction

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the predominant subtype of primary liver cancer, ranks as the sixth most commonly diagnosed malignancy and liver cancer remains the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide [<citation rid="B1-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/CM9.0000000000003264" pmid="39227359" pmcid="PMC11441870" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Its development is associated with various risk factors, such as the hepatitis B virus, alcohol consumption, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease [<citation rid="B2-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v28.i32.4540" pmid="36157932" pmcid="PMC9476877" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>China is a region with a high prevalence of the hepatitis B virus; the number of newly diagnosed cases of HCC in the country accounts for nearly half of the global total [<citation rid="B3-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3322/caac.21492" pmid="30207593" count="1">3</citation>,<citation rid="B4-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0140-6736(19)30427-1" pmid="31248666" pmcid="PMC6891889" count="1">4</citation>], underscoring the immense disease burden faced by this population. <sentence_start/>Current treatment modalities for HCC include liver transplantation, surgical resection, and local ablation. <sentence_start/>Although these therapies prove effective for a subset of patients, they are limited by high rates of recurrence and metastasis, resulting in suboptimal long-term survival outcomes [<citation rid="B5-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/SLA.0000000000001556" pmid="26813914" count="1">5</citation>].

Vascular invasion is a prominent pathological feature of HCC and an important determinant of prognosis [<citation rid="B6-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-23-2933" pmid="38470497" count="1">6</citation>], closely associated with tumor stage and disease progression. <sentence_start/>From a histological perspective, it can be classified into macrovascular invasion and microvascular invasion (MVI). <sentence_start/>Macrovascular invasion typically indicates a relatively advanced stage of the disease, often precluding surgical intervention, and is associated with a poor prognosis [<citation rid="B7-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/eci.13542" pmid="33755196" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast, MVI may appear during the early stages of the disease and holds greater clinical diagnostic significance [<citation rid="B8-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1245/s10434-019-07227-9" pmid="30788629" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although imaging techniques can detect major vascular invasion preoperatively, their limited resolution makes it difficult to reliably identify MVI. <sentence_start/>Currently, the diagnosis of MVI relies on postoperative tissue biopsy, an invasive procedure limited by the inherent variability of sample collection. <sentence_start/>The inherent shortcomings of these two detection methods have spurred extensive research into non-invasive alternatives.

Consequently, liquid biopsy is a highly promising non-invasive diagnostic tool. <sentence_start/>It shows considerable promise for the preoperative prediction of MVI, achieving this objective by capturing real-time tumor information. <sentence_start/>By analyzing tumor-derived components within bodily fluids including circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells (CTCs), circulating tumor RNA (ctRNA), and extracellular vesicles (EVs), it provides dynamic molecular insights that are unattainable through traditional tissue biopsies or static imaging. <sentence_start/>Its capacity for longitudinal monitoring, the avoidance of sampling bias, and the reflection of tumor heterogeneity further underscores its clinical value in preoperative assessment. <sentence_start/>However, current evidence primarily demonstrates significant associations between liquid biopsy signals and MVI-related aggressive tumor features, whereas the specific causal and MVI-specific relationships remain largely speculative and lack direct prospective validation. <sentence_start/>To address this gap, this review adopts a structured evidence-classification approach (see Table 1), categorizing each biomarker according to the level of direct support for MVI prediction, ranging from histopathologically confirmed MVI association to mechanistic plausibility based on general tumor aggressiveness.

Previous reviews have addressed individual aspects of MVI assessment. <sentence_start/>Radiomics-based reviews have focused on imaging features [<citation rid="B9-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00261-022-03496-3" pmid="35364684" count="1">9</citation>], such as tumor margin irregularity, peritumoral enhancement, and texture analysis, for preoperative MVI prediction, without integrating liquid biopsy biomarkers. <sentence_start/>Liquid biopsy reviews in HCC have primarily addressed diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring rather than MVI-specific prediction [<citation rid="B10-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2022.781820" pmid="35211399" pmcid="PMC8860830" count="1">10</citation>], and have rarely compared different analyte classes within a unified framework. <sentence_start/>Reviews on multi-omics predictive modeling have discussed general integration strategies without using MVI as the central organizational endpoint [<citation rid="B11-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12672-025-03623-8" pmid="41286162" pmcid="PMC12669466" count="1">11</citation>].

The present review differs from existing work in three respects. <sentence_start/>First, it adopts an MVI-centric framework that organizes evidence around histologically confirmed MVI as the primary endpoint, rather than aggregating all biomarker associations related to HCC aggressiveness or recurrence. <sentence_start/>Second, it provides a comparative evaluation of four liquid biopsy analyte categories, namely ctDNA, CTCs, ctRNA, and EVs, with each category assessed according to a standardized evidence-level classification (Level A, direct pathological validation of MVI; Level B, indirect association with vascular invasion evidence; Level C, aggressive tumor phenotype evidence; and Level D, mechanistic plausibility). <sentence_start/>Third, it explicitly outlines the translational pathway from biomarker discovery to multi-omics model integration and ultimately to potential risk-adapted clinical management, while clearly distinguishing currently available evidence from future validation requirements. <sentence_start/>By maintaining a consistent focus on MVI as the unifying endpoint, this review provides a structured synthesis that complements existing general reviews of liquid biopsy applications in HCC. <sentence_start/>As a narrative review, the objective is not to provide an exhaustive catalog of all published biomarkers or integrated prediction models. <sentence_start/>Rather, representative studies were selected to illustrate the major biomarker categories, methodological approaches, and stages of clinical development currently reported in the field.

This narrative review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of liquid biopsy biomarkers, including ctDNA, CTCs, ctRNA, and EVs, and their integration into multi-omics predictive models for the preoperative assessment of MVI in HCC. <sentence_start/>In addition, it explores the translational pathway from MVI risk stratification to individualized clinical management, with particular emphasis on the opportunities, current limitations, and future directions for clinical implementation (Figure 1).
2. <sentence_start/>Definition of MVI

Histologically, MVI is defined as the presence of tumor cell clusters within vascular lumina lined by endothelial cells, typically occurring in the peritumoral regions of surgically resected specimens [<citation rid="B34-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v22.i42.9279" pmid="27895416" pmcid="PMC5107692" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As a critical step in the process of tumor metastasis and dissemination, MVI begins with the detachment of invasive tumor cells from the primary site. <sentence_start/>These cells subsequently enter vascular channels and form tumor nests. <sentence_start/>These tumor nests may subsequently release CTCs into the bloodstream, thereby facilitating the formation of distant metastases (Figure 2).

Although MVI holds clear diagnostic significance in clinical practice, its diagnostic criteria remain subject to certain limitations due to variations in specimen sampling among pathologists, as well as inter-observer disagreement. <sentence_start/>These limitations in specimen sampling stem from early definitions regarding the portal or hepatic veins. <sentence_start/>Although Rodríguez-Peralvarez et al. later expanded the criteria to include arteries, arterioles, and lymphatics [<citation rid="B36-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1245/s10434-012-2513-1" pmid="23149850" count="1">36</citation>], this broader scope introduces additional variables into the selection of blood vessels. <sentence_start/>Inter-observer variability among pathologists further complicates the diagnostic process, as the interpretation of morphological features including tumor cluster size, the integrity of the endothelial lining, and proximity to the vascular lumen often varies significantly across different institutions [<citation rid="B37-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00432-016-2286-1" pmid="27743138" pmcid="PMC11819416" count="1">37</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To enhance diagnostic consistency and support clinical management, various MVI classification systems have been proposed. <sentence_start/>For instance, Roayaie et al. classified MVI into grades B1 through B3 based on the extent of muscular vascular invasion and its distance from the tumor [<citation rid="B38-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2009.06.003" pmid="19524573" pmcid="PMC2739450" count="1">38</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hwang et al. classified the severity of MVI (mild/severe) based on the number of invaded microvessels and tumor cells [<citation rid="B39-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3350/cmh.2023.0034" pmid="37157775" pmcid="PMC10366800" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In China, Cong et al. established a risk stratification system and incorporated it into national guidelines. <sentence_start/>This system classifies MVI into the following categories: (1) M0, defined as no MVI detected; (2) M1 (low-risk), defined as the presence of ≤5 MVI foci within the hepatic tissue surrounding the tumor (≤1 cm from the tumor edge); (3) M2 (high-risk), defined as the presence of >5 MVI foci or any MVI located in the distant peritumoral liver tissue (>1 cm from the tumor edge). <sentence_start/>This comprehensive framework integrates international and domestic data regarding HCC, establishing a unified definition of MVI for the first time in China [<citation rid="B40-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jhbp.303" pmid="26427066" pmcid="PMC12770223" count="1">40</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although these systems can enhance reporting consistency and facilitate risk stratification, their clinical utility remains constrained by issues regarding sample representativeness and challenges in pathological interpretation. <sentence_start/>Consequently, further validation is required to substantiate their relevance in terms of prognosis and treatment.
3. MVI Detection

Accurate preoperative assessment of MVI in HCC is crucial for formulating personalized clinical management and conducting prognostic assessments [<citation rid="B41-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1148/radiol.2019181818" pmid="31135299" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As an indicator of tumor aggressiveness, MVI is closely associated with postoperative recurrence and metastatic potential. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the early and reliable identification of MVI is of great clinical importance, yet it remains a challenge. <sentence_start/>Currently, the assessment of MVI primarily relies on postoperative histopathology and preoperative imaging-based assessment. <sentence_start/>In recent years, liquid biopsy has increasingly been incorporated into the assessment framework for MVI in HCC, serving as a complementary, minimally invasive, and reproducible approach alongside tissue-based histopathological assessment and imaging. <sentence_start/>The biomarkers obtained through liquid biopsy primarily include CTCs, ctDNA, ctRNA, and EVs carrying tumor-derived nucleic acids and proteins. <sentence_start/>Collectively, these markers provide biological insights into tumor aggressiveness, thereby offering the potential to improve the preoperative prediction of MVI, as well as to facilitate risk stratification and long-term monitoring in the postoperative setting.
4. Tissue Biopsy and Imaging for MVI Detection

Regarding the assessment of MVI, traditional methods include invasive tissue biopsy and non-invasive imaging techniques. <sentence_start/>Tissue biopsy enables histopathological evaluation and remains the gold standard for the diagnosis of MVI. <sentence_start/>It allows for the direct visualization of the interactions between the tumor and blood vessels, and possesses high diagnostic specificity. <sentence_start/>However, its clinical application is subject to several major limitations. <sentence_start/>First, biopsy specimens are typically obtained during surgery and evaluated postoperatively, which limits their utility in preoperative clinical management. <sentence_start/>Moreover, the accuracy of MVI detection is strongly influenced by sampling strategies. <sentence_start/>The number and spatial distribution of sampling sites (NuSS) directly influence the detection rate. <sentence_start/>The traditional four-point sampling method primarily targets the tumor center and a limited surrounding area, which may fail to adequately cover the interface between the tumor and the liver, thereby leading to missed detections of MVI. <sentence_start/>To overcome these limitations, the present updated guidelines recommend a standardized 7-point sampling protocol that includes additional peritumoral regions and achieves a higher MVI detection rate [<citation rid="B34-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v22.i42.9279" pmid="27895416" pmcid="PMC5107692" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Yet sampling errors and interpretive variability can still produce false-negative results [<citation rid="B42-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2023/5727701" pmid="37292454" pmcid="PMC10247321" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Second, pathological examination is central to the tissue-based assessment of MVI, with H&E staining and immunohistochemical markers (e.g., CD34 and CK19) supporting MVI identification [<citation rid="B37-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00432-016-2286-1" pmid="27743138" pmcid="PMC11819416" count="1">37</citation>,<citation rid="B43-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12957-022-02632-z" pmid="35725470" pmcid="PMC9210815" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, pathology is observer-dependent and largely morphology-based, providing static information that cannot capture dynamic molecular changes and has limited ability to predict recurrence patterns [<citation rid="B44-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/JHC.S438850" pmid="38737385" pmcid="PMC11088842" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="B45-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mco2.510" pmid="38463397" pmcid="PMC10924639" count="1">45</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Finally, beyond these methodological limitations, tissue biopsy also encounters several practical clinical constraints, including invasiveness, limited patient acceptance, poor support for real-time or preoperative evaluation. <sentence_start/>Therefore, more flexible and non-invasive approaches are needed to achieve the prediction of MVI.

Non-invasive imaging modalities, including computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), are widely explored for MVI evaluation [<citation rid="B46-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1148/radiol.222729" pmid="37097141" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Prior studies have reported multiple tumor imaging features associated with MVI [<citation rid="B47-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2214/AJR.10.4720" pmid="21512074" count="1">47</citation>,<citation rid="B48-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1148/radiol.2015150998" pmid="26653683" count="1">48</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, the reported correlations of specific features with MVI are often inconsistent, such as those related to tumor margin irregularity [<citation rid="B49-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000539380" pmid="40144472" pmcid="PMC11936442" count="1">49</citation>], reducing the clinical reliability of imaging-based assessment. <sentence_start/>Radiomics has emerged to address this gap by extracting high-dimensional imaging features for predictive modeling. <sentence_start/>Yet radiomics faces several challenges: (1) feature reproducibility remains poor due to inadequate standardization [<citation rid="B50-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/annonc/mdx034" pmid="28168275" count="1">50</citation>]; (2) few models have been developed for small HCCs, defined as tumors ≤3 cm in diameter [<citation rid="B51-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers14071816" pmid="35406589" pmcid="PMC8997857" count="1">51</citation>]; (3) combined models from single-center studies show limited clinical applicability due to lacking external validation [<citation rid="B52-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/liv.15254" pmid="35319151" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="B53-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2022.831996" pmid="35463303" pmcid="PMC9021380" count="1">53</citation>,<citation rid="B54-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-024-78467-3" pmid="39506070" pmcid="PMC11541849" count="1">54</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition, large-scale data processing and technical complexity hinder clinical translation.

Overall, traditional tissue biopsy and imaging techniques face limitations in providing real-time, preoperative, and biology-based assessments of MVI, as they rely primarily on static and indirect information. <sentence_start/>These shared limitations underscore the need for more flexible and actionable diagnostic strategies. <sentence_start/>In this context, liquid biopsy offers a promising alternative by enabling dynamic, preoperative, and molecularly informed evaluation of MVI.
5. <sentence_start/>Liquid Biopsy for MVI Detection

With the rise in minimally invasive diagnostics, liquid biopsy has become an important strategy for disease detection and monitoring. <sentence_start/>It refers to the analysis of body fluids, most commonly peripheral blood, to identify disease-related signals, particularly tumor-derived materials released into circulation during tumor growth, apoptosis, and necrosis [<citation rid="B55-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000499337" pmid="31091522" count="1">55</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The major analytes include ctDNA, CTCs, ctRNA, and EVs. <sentence_start/>All of which provide direct molecular evidence of tumor behavior. <sentence_start/>By providing accessible and repeatable molecular readouts, liquid biopsy complements tissue pathology and imaging, and is increasingly regarded as a key component of precision medicine for early detection, risk stratification, treatment selection, and longitudinal surveillance across oncology and other clinical fields.

As noted in the introduction, liquid biopsy offers unique advantages for MVI assessment, including non-invasiveness, real-time monitoring, and the capacity to capture tumor heterogeneity through serial blood sampling [<citation rid="B56-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1535-7163.MCT-22-0087" pmid="35545008" pmcid="PMC10314793" count="1">56</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Accumulating evidence has demonstrated significant associations between MVI status and specific circulating biomarkers, particularly CTCs and ctDNA [<citation rid="B57-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/liv.14463" pmid="32279416" pmcid="PMC7496978" count="1">57</citation>,<citation rid="B58-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12072-023-10540-x" pmid="37217808" count="1">58</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, the strength of evidence supporting individual biomarkers varies considerably. <sentence_start/>To facilitate systematic evaluation, we have adopted an evidence-level classification framework: Level A (direct MVI histopathological validation), Level B (indirect vascular invasion evidence), Level C (aggressive tumor phenotype evidence), and Level D (mechanistic plausibility). <sentence_start/>In the following sections, we will comprehensively summarize the evidence linking each biomarker to MVI and provide an overview of the primary analytical platforms utilized for their detection, with a particular emphasis on their respective clinical utility.
6. <sentence_start/>Circulating Tumor DNA (ctDNA)

ctDNA is a tumor-derived fraction of cell-free DNA (cfDNA), consisting of short DNA fragments released into the bloodstream mainly through tumor-cell apoptosis and necrosis, typically ~100-150 bp in length [<citation rid="B59-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2023.102595" pmid="37390697" count="1">59</citation>]. <sentence_start/>By sampling tumor signals from multiple lesions and subclones, ctDNA can partially mitigate the spatial heterogeneity and sampling bias inherent to tissue biopsy [<citation rid="B60-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/sj.onc.1208732" pmid="16007211" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Key ctDNA features, including somatic mutations, methylation signatures, and fragmentation patterns, have been investigated for their potential relevance to MVI and MVI-associated aggressive tumor phenotypes, although the strength of supporting evidence varies considerably. <sentence_start/>While some markers have been directly validated against histopathological MVI, many are supported primarily by indirect associations; the evidence level for individual ctDNA biomarkers is summarized in Table 1.
6.1. <sentence_start/>CtDNA Profiling

The mutational landscape captured by ctDNA reflects the aggressive biology of tumors. <sentence_start/>Higher ctDNA mutation burden has been associated with an increased risk of early postoperative recurrence (Level C) [<citation rid="B15-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12072-022-10348-1" pmid="35674872" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Direct evidence for MVI was provided by a prospective study of 41 patients, in which maximal ctDNA variant allele frequency (VAF) was significantly higher in MVI-positive than MVI-negative cases (0.038 versus 0.012; <italic>p</italic> = 0.0048), achieving an AUC of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.693-0.998) for preoperative MVI prediction (Level A) [<citation rid="B12-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2022.783109" pmid="35155229" pmcid="PMC8828586" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>TP53, KEAP1, HIST1H3D, NFKBIA, PIK3CB and WRN mutations, together with enrichment of Rap1 and Ras signaling pathways, were more frequent in MVI-positive tumors [<citation rid="B12-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2022.783109" pmid="35155229" pmcid="PMC8828586" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings support the potential of ctDNA-based genomic profiling for non-invasive MVI risk assessment, although larger validation cohorts are still needed.

DNA methylation represents a stable epigenetic layer with potential utility for MVI prediction. <sentence_start/>A genome-wide methylation study of 35 HCC patients identified an eight-MHB (methylation haplotype block) tissue methylation signature that predicted MVI with a cross-validated AUC of 85.9% and remained an independent predictor of MVI (OR = 47.51; <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) (Level A) [<citation rid="B13-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s40001-022-00910-w" pmid="36464701" pmcid="PMC9720918" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, the corresponding cfDNA methylation signature, despite achieving an AUC of 96.0% for HCC detection, failed to discriminate MVI status, limiting its current applicability as a liquid biopsy marker [<citation rid="B13-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s40001-022-00910-w" pmid="36464701" pmcid="PMC9720918" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In another retrospective cohort of 111 patients, plasma methylated SEPT9 (mSEPT9) was identified as an independent predictor of MVI (<italic>p</italic> = 0.002), with improved performance when combined with PIVKA-II (AUC = 0.72, sensitivity 62.1%, specificity 74.4%) (Level A) [<citation rid="B14-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/15330338221144510" pmid="36573042" pmcid="PMC9806378" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These data indicate that methylation signatures may contribute to both preoperative MVI prediction and prognostic assessment.

CtDNA fragmentation patterns. <sentence_start/>Beyond mutations and methylation, ctDNA fragmentation features, including fragment size, end motifs and nucleosome footprints, provide complementary information on tumor biology [<citation rid="B61-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1272-6" pmid="31142840" pmcid="PMC6774252" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In a recent shallow whole-genome sequencing (sWGS) study of 134 patients with advanced HCC, elevated cfDNA fragmentation (>28%) was significantly associated with multinodularity (<italic>p</italic> = 0.02) and portal vein thrombosis (<italic>p</italic> = 0.003), representing indirect evidence of vascular invasion (Level B) [<citation rid="B16-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejca.2025.115633" pmid="40763617" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although direct associations with histopathologically confirmed MVI have not yet been established, the link between fragmentomic features and macrovascular invasion, together with their independent prognostic value, highlights ctDNA fragmentomics as a promising non-invasive biomarker that merits dedicated MVI-focused validation studies.
6.2. <sentence_start/>CtDNA Analysis Technologies

Depending on the specific genomic regions of interest, ctDNA analysis techniques are generally categorized into targeted and non-targeted methods. <sentence_start/>The former screens for mutations within a pre-defined set of genes (e.g., single nucleotide variants), while the latter explores genomic aberrations (e.g., WGS). <sentence_start/>Targeted methods include droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) [<citation rid="B62-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00535-021-01773-4" pmid="33712873" count="1">62</citation>], beads, emulsion, amplification, and magnetics (BEAMing) [<citation rid="B63-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.1789" pmid="18670422" pmcid="PMC2820391" count="1">63</citation>], safe-sequencing system (Safe-SeqS) [<citation rid="B64-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/scitranslmed.aaf6219" pmid="27384348" pmcid="PMC5346159" count="1">64</citation>], cancer personalized profiling by deep sequencing (CAPP-Seq), and tagged amplicon deep sequencing (TAm-Seq) [<citation rid="B65-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/scitranslmed.3003726" pmid="22649089" count="1">65</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These technologies possess extremely high sensitivity (with a detection limit for mutant allele frequencies as low as 0.01%) and high specificity for known mutations; they are, therefore, highly suitable for monitoring treatment responses in MVI patients [<citation rid="B66-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/pds.5768" pmid="38419132" count="1">66</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, their reliance on prior knowledge of mutations limits the discovery of novel biomarkers [<citation rid="B67-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.foodres.2023.113502" pmid="37986417" count="1">67</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Untargeted methods primarily involve next-generation sequencing (NGS) which provide comprehensive genomic profiling, such as whole exome sequencing (WES) and WGS [<citation rid="B68-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers13092229" pmid="34066484" pmcid="PMC8125351" count="1">68</citation>,<citation rid="B69-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3350/cmh.2023.0426" pmid="38163441" pmcid="PMC11016491" count="1">69</citation>], but face challenges in sensitivity and cost-effectiveness for routine MVI screening [<citation rid="B70-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijns8030040" pmid="35892470" pmcid="PMC9326745" count="1">70</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Based on enrichment strategies, NGS-based techniques are further classified as targeted amplification sequencing (TAS) and targeted capture sequencing (TCS). <sentence_start/>These technologies enable the simultaneous assessment of multiple molecular features and therefore hold considerable potential for preoperative MVI evaluation [<citation rid="B71-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.21037/qims-24-44" pmid="39022260" pmcid="PMC11250313" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, although some studies have reported direct associations with histopathologically confirmed MVI, much of the current evidence remains derived from correlations with aggressive tumor characteristics and clinical outcomes, highlighting the need for further prospective validation. <sentence_start/>In addition, while NGS facilitates the noninvasive characterization of tumor heterogeneity, persistent challenges remain in assay standardization, data interpretation, and the discrimination of authentic tumor-derived signals from sequencing artifacts [<citation rid="B72-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cca.2023.117568" pmid="37839516" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Specific detection methods can be found in Table 2 [<citation rid="B73-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ctm2.1014" pmid="35998020" pmcid="PMC9398227" count="1">73</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Classifications of current detection technologies are presented in Figure 3.
6.3. <sentence_start/>Confounding Factors in Liquid Biopsy Interpretation

The interpretation of circulating biomarkers for MVI prediction must account for several biological and clinical factors that can influence liquid biopsy measurements independently of MVI status. <sentence_start/>Liver cirrhosis, present in the majority of HCC patients and particularly prevalent in Asian populations, elevates background cfDNA levels through chronic hepatocyte turnover and may alter DNA methylation patterns independently of tumor biology [<citation rid="B92-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/gutjnl-2016-311526" pmid="27002005" pmcid="PMC5031527" count="1">92</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Active viral hepatitis, particularly during alanine aminotransferase (ALT) flares, can cause non-specific cfDNA release from inflamed but non-malignant hepatocytes, potentially confounding ctDNA-based MVI prediction [<citation rid="B93-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v25.i29.3985" pmid="31413532" pmcid="PMC6689808" count="1">93</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Prior locoregional therapy, including transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) and radiofrequency ablation (RFA), induces tumor necrosis that transiently elevates ctDNA levels, complicating the interpretation of post-treatment liquid biopsy measurements [<citation rid="B62-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00535-021-01773-4" pmid="33712873" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Systemic therapies, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors, can modulate CTC counts and phenotypes through both anti-tumor effects and off-target hematopoietic alterations [<citation rid="B94-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/hep4.1577" pmid="33024921" pmcid="PMC7527695" count="1">94</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, background liver injury, steatohepatitis, and systemic inflammation may alter EV composition and ctRNA profiles independently of MVI [<citation rid="B95-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrgastro.2017.71" pmid="28634412" pmcid="PMC6380505" count="1">95</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hemolysis during blood collection releases erythrocyte-derived miRNAs that can dominate small RNA sequencing libraries and mask tumor-derived signals [<citation rid="B96-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0024145" pmid="21909417" pmcid="PMC3164711" count="1">96</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These confounders underscore the critical importance of well-characterized control populations with documented liver disease etiology, severity, treatment history, and inflammatory status when evaluating liquid biopsy-based MVI prediction. <sentence_start/>Standardized reporting of these clinical variables should be adopted in future studies to enable meaningful cross-study comparisons.
7. Circulating Tumor Cells (CTCs)

CTCs are cancer cells that detach from primary solid tumors, intravasate into the bloodstream or lymphatic system, and may eventually form metastases in distant organs. <sentence_start/>In HCC, both the presence and biological characteristics of CTCs have important clinical implications and have been associated with tumor progression, metastatic potential, and MVI [<citation rid="B18-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ebiom.2020.103107" pmid="33181461" pmcid="PMC7658489" count="1">18</citation>,<citation rid="B97-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-24-4323" pmid="40794711" pmcid="PMC12485388" count="1">97</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Given the marked heterogeneity of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in both biological characteristics and abundance, CTC-based analyses are generally approached from two complementary perspectives: phenotypic profiling and quantitative assessment. <sentence_start/>Based on the expression of epithelial and mesenchymal markers, CTCs can be broadly classified into epithelial, mesenchymal, and hybrid epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) phenotypes, reflecting varying degrees of cellular plasticity associated with tumor dissemination and metastatic potential. <sentence_start/>Among circulating biomarkers, CTCs, particularly mesenchymal and hybrid EMT phenotypes, provide relatively direct cellular evidence of vascular dissemination relevant to MVI. <sentence_start/>However, the strength of supporting evidence varies considerably across individual CTC biomarkers and study designs, as summarized in Table 1.

As discussed in ctDNA, confounding clinical factors, including liver disease etiology, prior locoregional therapy, and systemic treatment, should be carefully considered when interpreting CTC data for MVI prediction.
7.1. <sentence_start/>CTCs Phenotypic Profiling

Epithelial-phenotype CTCs (E-CTCs), characterized by the expression of epithelial markers such as EpCAM and cytokeratins, are generally considered to indicate the shedding of tumor cells from the primary lesion site. <sentence_start/>Clinical studies have confirmed a positive correlation between E-CTCs and tumor burden (r = 0.456, <italic>p</italic> = 0.008) [<citation rid="B22-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12072-016-9732-7" pmid="27115761" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Elevated E-CTC levels are associated with adverse treatment outcomes in HCC patients [<citation rid="B98-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13046-018-0893-1" pmid="30176913" pmcid="PMC6122633" count="1">98</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, direct evidence demonstrating that E-CTCs can serve as specific preoperative biomarkers for MVI remains limited (Level C).

Mesenchymal-phenotype CTCs (M-CTCs), representing tumor cells that have undergone EMT and therefore exhibit enhanced motility and invasiveness [<citation rid="B99-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.analchem.2c02416" pmid="36279553" count="1">99</citation>], have demonstrated predictive value for postoperative recurrence [<citation rid="B19-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00432-022-04526-9" pmid="36633681" pmcid="PMC10356895" count="1">19</citation>] and correlate with metastatic risk and adverse clinicopathological features, including elevated AFP levels, advanced tumor stage, and vascular invasion [<citation rid="B22-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12072-016-9732-7" pmid="27115761" count="1">22</citation>,<citation rid="B100-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijms222313073" pmid="34884878" pmcid="PMC8657934" count="1">100</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In a prospective study of 127 HCC patients, M-CTC percentage was positively correlated with MVI status (<italic>p</italic> = 0.0076) (Level A) [<citation rid="B19-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00432-022-04526-9" pmid="36633681" pmcid="PMC10356895" count="1">19</citation>], suggesting that the mesenchymal CTC phenotype may reflect aggressive tumor behavior relevant to MVI-associated invasion patterns.

EMT-phenotype CTCs (EMT-CTCs), characterized by the downregulation of epithelial markers (e.g., EpCAM/CK) and the upregulation of mesenchymal markers (e.g., vimentin), represent hybrid subpopulations capturing dynamic intermediate states during tumor progression [<citation rid="B101-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.drup.2024.101119" pmid="39111134" count="1">101</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Higher detection rates of vimentin-positive CTCs have been observed in patients with portal vein invasion (Level B) [<citation rid="B20-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/lt.25062" pmid="29624843" pmcid="PMC6097911" count="1">20</citation>], and twist/vimentin co-expression has been associated with portal vein tumor thrombus, TNM stage, and tumor size (Level B) [<citation rid="B21-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/cddis.2013.347" pmid="24091674" pmcid="PMC3824657" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although these findings support a potential relationship between EMT-related CTC phenotypes and vascular invasive behavior, direct evidence linking specific CTC subtypes to MVI remains insufficient and warrants further prospective validation.
7.2. <sentence_start/>Quantitative Assessment of CTC

Quantitative CTC enumeration provides one of the strongest evidence bases for preoperative MVI prediction. <sentence_start/>In a prospective study of 137 HCC patients, a preoperative CTC count ≥ 5/5 mL was an independent predictor of MVI (AUC = 0.856, sensitivity 91.4%, specificity 79.7%), outperforming both tumor diameter (AUC = 0.604) and AFP (AUC = 0.636); the multi-parameter combination (CTC + AFP + tumor diameter) achieved an AUC of 0.900 (Level A) [<citation rid="B17-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12885-020-07488-8" pmid="33129301" pmcid="PMC7603758" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A separate retrospective study of 309 HCC patients further demonstrated that preoperative CTC count positively correlated with MVI counts (r = 0.655; <italic>p</italic> < 0.001) and the farthest MVI distance from the tumor margin (r = 0.495; <italic>p</italic> < 0.001), and that CTC-positive patients specifically benefited from a surgical margin > 1 cm for protection against early recurrence (HR = 0.20-0.47) (Level A) [<citation rid="B18-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ebiom.2020.103107" pmid="33181461" pmcid="PMC7658489" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These studies collectively establish quantitative CTC assessment as one of the most clinically advanced liquid biopsy strategies for preoperative MVI evaluation, although the reliance on EpCAM-based capture in one study may underestimate the contribution of EMT-CTCs [<citation rid="B18-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ebiom.2020.103107" pmid="33181461" pmcid="PMC7658489" count="1">18</citation>].
7.3. <sentence_start/>CTCs Analysis Technologies

According to their isolation principles, current CTC analysis technologies are generally classified into immunoaffinity, physical, and hybrid methods. <sentence_start/>Immunoaffinity methods primarily rely on EpCAM-based antigen-antibody interactions, as exemplified by the FDA-approved CellSearch system [<citation rid="B74-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.critrevonc.2018.12.004" pmid="30771872" count="1">74</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The primary advantage of this method lies in its high specificity for epithelial CTCs and the reliability of its clinical validation. <sentence_start/>However, a major limitation is its inability to capture EMT-CTCs due to EpCAM downregulation during EMT, severely restricts its utility in MVI prediction where mesenchymal and hybrid CTCs phenotypes may be of particular importance [<citation rid="B102-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fchem.2024.1400988" pmid="38831912" pmcid="PMC11144890" count="1">102</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Physical techniques (including microfiltration, and density gradient centrifugation) offer the advantage of marker-independent CTCs isolation, potentially capturing the full spectrum of CTCs heterogeneity [<citation rid="B103-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/hep.20091" pmid="14999698" count="1">103</citation>], Nevertheless, these methods suffer from lower purity due to leukocyte contamination and may compromise cell viability through mechanical stress [<citation rid="B104-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jcyt.2024.10.002" pmid="39480386" count="1">104</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To enhance detection efficiency, a hybrid strategy combining physical enrichment with immunoaffinity validation (e.g., molecular characterization) represents the most promising method for detecting MVI [<citation rid="B105-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2016/1427849" pmid="27403030" pmcid="PMC4925990" count="1">105</citation>], thereby enabling the functional analysis of captured EMT-CTCs. <sentence_start/>However, barriers related to standardization, as well as technical complexities, have hindered clinical translation, particularly in the context of CTC subpopulations associated with rare MVI [<citation rid="B106-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/biomedicines12092137" pmid="39335650" pmcid="PMC11429165" count="1">106</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Specific detection methods can be found in Table 2 [<citation rid="B75-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.analchem.3c00143" pmid="37348197" count="1">75</citation>,<citation rid="B76-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/cam4.3790" pmid="33675149" pmcid="PMC7982624" count="1">76</citation>,<citation rid="B77-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/hep4.1900" pmid="35068084" pmcid="PMC9134808" count="1">77</citation>,<citation rid="B78-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.analchem.0c03936" pmid="33124804" count="1">78</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Classifications of current CTCs detection technologies are presented in Figure 4.
8. <sentence_start/>Circulating Tumor RNA (ctRNA) and Extracellular Vesicles (EVs)

The cell-free RNA (cfRNA) refers to RNA released into circulation by cells through death, necrosis or active secretion [<citation rid="B107-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2023.1134445" pmid="37091184" pmcid="PMC10115432" count="1">107</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The ctRNA, a tumor-derived subset of cfRNA, comprises coding RNAs (e.g., mRNA fragments) and non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). <sentence_start/>The latter encompasses microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs). <sentence_start/>The ctRNA contributes to cancer progression by regulating key processes, including cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and apoptosis. <sentence_start/>Its circulatory stability, tissue-specific expression, and capacity to distinguish between malignant and non-malignant lesions make it an attractive class of biomarker for liquid biopsy [<citation rid="B108-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41698-022-00270-y" pmid="35468987" pmcid="PMC9038724" count="1">108</citation>].

EVs including exosomes, microvesicles, and apoptotic bodies are lipid bilayer-enclosed vesicles with a diameter ranging from approximately 50 nm to more than 1000 nm that carry nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids [<citation rid="B109-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11427-024-2937-4" pmid="40650813" count="1">109</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Through systemic dissemination, EVs mediate intercellular communication and contribute to tumor progression and metastasis [<citation rid="B110-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cells9010130" pmid="31935901" pmcid="PMC7017260" count="1">110</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Their ability to encapsulate both nucleic acids and proteins from parent tumor cells makes them particularly valuable for liquid biopsy applications. <sentence_start/>In HCC, tumor-derived EVs can deliver oncogenic RNA to recipient cells, promoting tumor growth and invasion [<citation rid="B111-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/hep.24504" pmid="21721029" pmcid="PMC3310362" count="1">111</citation>]. <sentence_start/>While EV-associated proteins also reflect molecular features relevant to metastatic behavior [<citation rid="B112-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13578-024-01294-6" pmid="39227992" pmcid="PMC11373138" count="1">112</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Collectively, these characteristics underpin the growing interest in both EV-carried RNA (including mRNA and ncRNA) and EV proteomic signatures as potential biomarkers for MVI. <sentence_start/>As with other emerging circulating analytes, the evidence supporting the relevance of ctRNA and EV biomarkers to MVI spans a spectrum from direct pathological correlation to indirect clinical associations and mechanistic plausibility; this evidence gradient is systematically summarized in Table 1.

As discussed in ctDNA, the interpretation of ctRNA and EV biomarkers for MVI prediction must account for confounding factors including liver disease etiology, treatment history, and pre-analytical variables such as hemolysis, which can substantially alter circulating RNA profiles.
8.1. <sentence_start/>CtRNA Profiling

miRNAs are short ncRNAs characterized by high stability and resistance to degradation, making them attractive candidates as liquid biopsy biomarkers [<citation rid="B113-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12967-025-06941-1" pmid="40804405" pmcid="PMC12351995" count="1">113</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Among the strongest Level A evidence for ctRNA-based MVI prediction, serum miR-125b was identified as an independent predictor of MVI in a cohort of 108 HCC patients; when combined with tumor size and AFP, the predictive model achieved an AUC of 0.867 (sensitivity 72.37%, specificity 84.38%) [<citation rid="B23-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tranon.2016.03.002" pmid="27267832" pmcid="PMC4856864" count="1">23</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Mechanistically, angiogenesis, known to correlate closely with MVI [<citation rid="B114-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrc2621" pmid="19308068" pmcid="PMC3682494" count="1">114</citation>], may be facilitated by decreased miR-497, which derepresses VEGFA and AEG-1 to promote vascular endothelial signaling in HCC (Level D) [<citation rid="B24-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.5012" pmid="26336827" pmcid="PMC4745744" count="1">24</citation>].

lncRNAs, typically longer than 200 nucleotides, possess stable secondary structures that support their detectability in circulating fluids [<citation rid="B115-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.lfs.2024.122544" pmid="38458555" count="1">115</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Plasma lncRNAs XLOC_014172 and LOC149086 were significant upregulated in metastatic HCC patients, yielding AUC of 0.900 (training set) and 0.934 (validation set) for MVI prediction; however, the endpoint was broadly defined as metastasis rather than MVI-specific, placing this evidence at Level C [<citation rid="B25-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.2934" pmid="25714016" pmcid="PMC4414207" count="1">25</citation>].

circRNAs are covalently closed RNA molecules that regulate cancer progression by modulating signaling pathways and functioning as oncogenes or tumor suppressors [<citation rid="B116-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.critrevonc.2025.104942" pmid="40953760" count="1">116</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Prior research have studied that serum circSETD3 was identified as an independent risk factor for MVI (OR = 0.458; <italic>p</italic> = 0.009), with an AUC of 0.637 alone and 0.736 (95% CI: 0.628-0.844) when combined with PIVKA-II (Level A) [<citation rid="B26-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.21037/atm.2020.02.134" pmid="32355782" pmcid="PMC7186655" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Tissue-based studies have also demonstrated that elevated circ_0008934 expression is significantly associated with MVI (<italic>p</italic> = 0.008), functioning through the miR-1305/TMTC3 axis to promote proliferation and metastasis (Level C, tissue-based) [<citation rid="B27-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13577-021-00657-2" pmid="35015267" count="1">27</citation>].

mRNAs, especially when integrated with proteomic analysis, enhance the accuracy of cancer detection and characterization [<citation rid="B117-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mcpro.2023.100587" pmid="37290530" pmcid="PMC10388586" count="1">117</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Serum S100P mRNA, integrating transcriptomic and proteomic analysis, was highly expressed in 92.9% (183/197) of HCC tissues, with further elevation in PVTT and MVI cases; serum S100P protein predicted MVI preoperatively with an AUC of 0.744 (sensitivity 62.4%, specificity 83.0%) across a large combined retrospective and prospective cohort of 826 patients (Level A) [<citation rid="B28-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12072-020-10130-1" pmid="33495903" count="1">28</citation>].
8.2. <sentence_start/>EV Profiling

EV-encapsulated RNAs are protected by the vesicular lipid bilayer, conferring enhanced stability in blood and enabling sensitive detection while potentially capturing tumor heterogeneity [<citation rid="B118-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acsnano.4c01310" pmid="38628141" count="1">118</citation>,<citation rid="B119-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.aca.2024.342959" pmid="39122286" count="1">119</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A recent prospective study of 131 HCC patients demonstrated that plasma exosomal PRPSAP1 levels were significantly higher in patients with >5 MVI foci compared with those without MVI (0.147 versus 0.070; <italic>p</italic> = 0.035), providing direct evidence linking exosomal mRNA to MVI status (Level A) [<citation rid="B29-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jgh.16677" pmid="38972728" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, the overall MVI-positive versus MVI-negative comparison did not reach statistical significance for any single exosomal mRNA, indicating that the discriminatory power of this approach is currently restricted to high-MVI-burden disease. <sentence_start/>Several studies have reported dysregulated exosomal miRNA profiles in HCC, including altered expression of miR-21-5p, miR-10b-5p, miR-221-3p, and miR-718. <sentence_start/>Although these molecules are associated with tumor aggressiveness and recurrence risk, direct evidence verifying their relationship with MVI is lacking (Level C) [<citation rid="B30-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/bjc.2014.621" pmid="25584485" pmcid="PMC4453648" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="B31-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/emm.2015.68" pmid="26380927" pmcid="PMC4650928" count="1">31</citation>,<citation rid="B120-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ijc.33111" pmid="32441313" count="1">120</citation>].

Exosomal proteomics, reflecting the molecular composition and metastatic propensity of the parent tumor, also provides candidate biomarkers in HCC. <sentence_start/>Adenylate cyclase-associated protein 1 (CAP1), enriched in exosomes from highly metastatic HCC cell lines, correlates with metastatic propensity, and insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) enrichment in biomechanical stress-induced exosomes promotes migratory signaling via the Ras/Raf/ERK pathway; both currently remain at the mechanistic plausibility level (Level D) [<citation rid="B32-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.62347/OHTF9780" pmid="41244125" pmcid="PMC12616160" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3892/ol.2017.7257" pmid="29250190" pmcid="PMC5727617" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Collectively, EV-based biomarkers for MVI are at an earlier stage of clinical development compared with ctDNA- and CTC-based approaches, and most findings should be regarded as preliminary associations requiring confirmation in larger, MVI-focused prospective studies.
8.3. <sentence_start/>Analysis Technologies for ctRNA and EVs

In the analysis of ctRNA, analytical strategies are primarily designed according to the readout format and assay objective, and can be broadly classified into amplification-based quantitative techniques and capture-based sequencing techniques. <sentence_start/>Amplification-based methods include reverse-transcription droplet digital PCR (RT-ddPCR), which enables ultra-sensitive detection of low-abundance transcripts [<citation rid="B79-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-18311-0" pmid="32895384" pmcid="PMC7477161" count="1">79</citation>,<citation rid="B80-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/advs.202410120" pmid="39556692" pmcid="PMC11727120" count="1">80</citation>], and quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR), a rapid and cost-effective option for routine measurement [<citation rid="B81-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41420-021-00664-0" pmid="34599150" pmcid="PMC8486831" count="1">81</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast, capture-based platforms such as targeted RNA sequencing (Target-RNAseq) provide multiplexed analysis of predefined transcript panels [<citation rid="B82-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000545366" pmid="40331063" pmcid="PMC12052365" count="1">82</citation>], supporting downstream identification of expression signatures relevant to MVI.

In the analysis of EVs, methodological workflows typically involve multiple sequential steps. <sentence_start/>Based on the key analytical objectives, EV analysis encompasses isolation, characterization, and molecular profiling. <sentence_start/>Isolation techniques include ultracentrifugation (accessible but time-consuming/impractical) [<citation rid="B83-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhep.2021.12.005" pmid="34922977" count="1">83</citation>], size-exclusion chromatography (SEC; relatively pure plasma EVs are rapid but yield-limited) [<citation rid="B84-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jev2.12122" pmid="34429857" pmcid="PMC8363909" count="1">84</citation>], affinity capture (specific but potentially biased) [<citation rid="B85-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.xcrm.2024.101716" pmid="39241773" pmcid="PMC11525029" count="1">85</citation>], or emerging methods like microfluidics enhancing efficiency [<citation rid="B86-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bios.2025.117228" pmid="39954520" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Characterization uses electron microscopy [<citation rid="B87-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.yexcr.2022.113232" pmid="35659970" count="1">87</citation>], nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) [<citation rid="B88-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/JHC.S423043" pmid="37936599" pmcid="PMC10627088" count="1">88</citation>] and flow cytometry [<citation rid="B89-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/all.13234" pmid="28649804" count="1">89</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Molecular profiling shows significant potential, with EV proteomics aiding cancer detection [<citation rid="B90-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/hep.32692" pmid="35908246" pmcid="PMC9887095" count="1">90</citation>,<citation rid="B121-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/pmic.202000094" pmid="33665903" count="1">121</citation>] and small RNA sequencing (Small RNA-seq) revealing functional EV RNA cargo [<citation rid="B91-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/aging.103824" pmid="32269736" pmcid="PMC7137059" count="1">91</citation>].

For MVI diagnostics, these platforms offer non-invasive discovery of vascular invasion biomarkers via ctRNA/EV-derived molecules, yet critical translation challenges persist: detecting ultra-low abundance MVI signatures, standardizing pre-analytical variables (especially EV isolation), validating specificity against background noise and non-MVI HCC, scaling complex protocols clinically, and conducting large prospective studies correlating liquid biopsy findings with histopathology. <sentence_start/>Specific detection methods can be found in Table 2. <sentence_start/>Classifications of current EV detection technologies are presented in Figure 5.

Recent advances in liquid biopsy have enabled increasing exploration of circulating biomarkers for the preoperative prediction of MVI in HCC. <sentence_start/>Existing studies indicate that ctDNA, CTCs, ctRNAs, and EVs reflect complementary aspects of tumor burden, vascular dissemination, and invasion-related molecular programs associated with MVI. <sentence_start/>However, the level of clinical evidence supporting individual biomarkers varies considerably across analyte classes and study designs. <sentence_start/>To address this heterogeneity, we propose an evidence-level classification framework that stratifies reported biomarkers according to the strength and directness of their MVI validation (Table 1): Level A, Level B, Level C, and Level D. This evidence-based framework reveals a notable translational gradient: ctDNA- and CTC-based markers have accumulated the highest level of evidence through direct histopathological correlation [<citation rid="B57-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/liv.14463" pmid="32279416" pmcid="PMC7496978" count="1">57</citation>,<citation rid="B58-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12072-023-10540-x" pmid="37217808" count="1">58</citation>], whereas the majority of ctRNA and EV-derived biomarkers remain at exploratory evidence levels (C-D), indicating a pressing need for prospective validation studies with MVI-specific endpoints. <sentence_start/>The evidence-level classification of individual biomarkers is detailed in Table 1, and a systematic overview of available detection methodologies is provided in Table 2.
9. <sentence_start/>Pre-Analytical and Analytical Considerations

The reliability and comparability of liquid biopsy-based MVI prediction depend critically on standardization across the entire workflow, from blood collection to data analysis. <sentence_start/>Current studies exhibit substantial methodological heterogeneity that limits cross-study comparisons and impedes clinical translation.

Blood collection and processing. <sentence_start/>The choice of blood collection tube significantly affects cfDNA yield and stability. <sentence_start/>EDTA tubes require processing within 2-4 h to prevent leukocyte lysis and genomic DNA contamination, whereas specialized cell-free DNA blood collection tubes (BCTs) stabilize cfDNA for up to 48 h at room temperature through proprietary preservatives [<citation rid="B122-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmoldx.2018.07.005" pmid="30165204" pmcid="PMC6197164" count="1">122</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For CTC analysis, the time from venipuncture to processing affects cell viability and surface marker expression; processing delays exceeding 4 h have been associated with reduced CTC recovery and altered phenotypic marker profiles [<citation rid="B123-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1475-2867-14-23" pmid="24602297" pmcid="PMC3995911" count="1">123</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For EV studies, the collection tube type, anticoagulant, and processing delay influence vesicle integrity, concentration, and cargo composition [<citation rid="B124-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jev2.12315" pmid="37202906" pmcid="PMC10196222" count="1">124</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Standardization of collection and initial processing protocols is therefore a prerequisite for cross-study reproducibility.

Centrifugation and storage. <sentence_start/>Standardized two-step centrifugation (typically 1600× <italic>g</italic> for 10 min at 4 °C followed by 16,000× <italic>g</italic> for 10 min at 4 °C) is recommended for plasma preparation to minimize residual cellular debris, though protocols vary substantially across published MVI studies [<citation rid="B125-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2018.e00699" pmid="30094369" pmcid="PMC6074610" count="1">125</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Plasma storage at −80 °C is standard, but freeze-thaw cycles degrade ctRNA and may alter EV morphology and cargo. <sentence_start/>A maximum of one freeze-thaw cycle should be maintained, and aliquoting upon initial processing is strongly recommended to avoid repeated thawing.

Extraction and isolation methods. <sentence_start/>For cfDNA, silica column-based kits and magnetic bead-based methods show variable recovery efficiency depending on fragment size, with potential bias toward shorter or longer fragments [<citation rid="B126-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/clinchem/hvac069" pmid="35616097" count="1">126</citation>]. <sentence_start/>EV isolation methods differ substantially: ultracentrifugation yields high-purity preparations but is time-intensive and operator-dependent; SEC provides relatively pure plasma EVs rapidly but at lower yield; polymer-based precipitation offers convenience but co-isolates non-EV contaminants including lipoproteins and protein aggregates; immunoaffinity capture achieves high specificity for selected surface markers but may miss subpopulations lacking the target antigen [<citation rid="B127-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/20013078.2018.1535750" pmid="30637094" pmcid="PMC6322352" count="1">127</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These methodological differences directly affect downstream molecular profiling and must be carefully considered when comparing results across studies.

Detection platforms and bioinformatics. <sentence_start/>Digital PCR offers high sensitivity for known targets with absolute quantification but limited multiplexing capacity. <sentence_start/>NGS enables broad genomic, transcriptomic, or methylomic profiling but introduces technical variability related to sequencing depth, library preparation protocols, alignment algorithms, and variant-calling pipelines [<citation rid="B128-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/clinchem/hvaa164" pmid="32870995" pmcid="PMC7462123" count="1">128</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The choice of platform and bioinformatics workflow can substantially influence the detection of low-abundance MVI-associated signals, and inter-laboratory harmonization efforts are urgently needed.

Hemolysis. <sentence_start/>Hemolysis during blood collection or processing releases erythrocyte-derived miRNAs and other cellular RNAs that can dominate sequencing libraries and mask tumor-derived signals. <sentence_start/>Spectrophotometric assessment of hemolysis (e.g., absorbance measurement at 414 nm for hemoglobin) should be routinely reported in ctRNA and EV studies, and samples with moderate-to-severe hemolysis should be excluded or analyzed with appropriate correction algorithms [<citation rid="B129-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1940-6207.CAPR-11-0370" pmid="22158052" pmcid="PMC4186243" count="1">129</citation>].

In summary, until these pre-analytical and analytical variables are harmonized through consensus protocols and inter-laboratory validation studies, the clinical implementation of liquid biopsy-based MVI prediction will remain aspirational. <sentence_start/>Future studies should adopt standardized reporting frameworks, such as the BIOSPECIMEN Reporting for Improved Study Quality (BRISQ) guidelines, to facilitate meaningful data integration and meta-analysis [<citation rid="B130-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/pr200021n" pmid="21574648" pmcid="PMC3169291" count="1">130</citation>].
10. <sentence_start/>Liquid Biopsy Models for MVI Prediction

The use of liquid biopsy for the preoperative risk assessment of MVI has gradually garnered attention due to its potential value in clinical management. <sentence_start/>However, its primary value lies in biologically grounded risk stratification, rather than in directly guiding clinical management selection. <sentence_start/>Quantitative ctDNA metrics enable the classification of high- and low-risk MVI populations [<citation rid="B57-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/liv.14463" pmid="32279416" pmcid="PMC7496978" count="1">57</citation>], while CTCs, ctRNAs, and EVs provide complementary evidence of vascular invasion and aggressive tumor behavior. <sentence_start/>It is important to recognize that the individual biomarkers feeding into these models differ substantially in their evidence strength for MVI prediction, as categorized in Table 1; models incorporating biomarkers with direct MVI validation should be weighted differently in clinical interpretation than those relying primarily on indirect or mechanistic associations.

Although these biomarkers demonstrate a significant association with MVI, the majority of current studies still rely on a single-marker approach. <sentence_start/>Such strategies are constrained by tumor heterogeneity, inter-individual variability, and the low abundance of circulating analytes, resulting in suboptimal predictive performance. <sentence_start/>To address these limitations, recent studies have increasingly adopted integrative strategies. <sentence_start/>These strategies involve combining multiple liquid biopsy markers or integrating clinicopathological and imaging data to develop more robust predictive models [<citation rid="B131-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.critrevonc.2023.104107" pmid="37633349" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Such methods improve the accuracy and reliability of preoperative MVI assessment.

This section reviews comprehensive models based on liquid biopsy, which can be categorized into three types: multi-marker liquid biopsy models, liquid biopsy-clinicopathological integration models, and liquid biopsy-imaging integration models. <sentence_start/>By moving beyond single biomarkers to enhance the accuracy of MVI risk stratification, these models provide a quantitative reference for risk assessment and enable intuitive risk stratification: MVI-negative patients are defined as low-risk, while MVI-positive patients are categorized as high-risk per clinical guidelines. <sentence_start/>This stratification may provide a quantitative reference basis for personalized clinical management of HCC.
Before discussing specific models, it is useful to classify current liquid biopsy-based prediction models according to their stage of clinical readiness:

Exploratory models: Derived from single-center retrospective data with internal validation only (e.g., cross-validation or split-sample validation). <sentence_start/>While reported AUC values provide proof-of-concept, these models are not yet suitable for clinical application due to unproven generalizability.

Validation candidates: Models that have undergone external validation in one or more independent cohorts. <sentence_start/>These warrant prospective evaluations but have not yet demonstrated clinical utility in real-world settings.

Potential clinical tools: Models validated in multicenter prospective studies, with decision-curve analysis demonstrating clinical net benefit, predefined and validated risk thresholds, and evidence of transportability across populations and healthcare settings. <sentence_start/>At present, no liquid biopsy-based MVI prediction model has reached this level of maturity.

This framework provides the basis for critically evaluating the representative models discussed in the following subsections. <sentence_start/>Reported performance metrics should be interpreted in light of each model’s stage of development, while recognizing that the models highlighted here are intended to illustrate the current state of the field rather than provide an exhaustive catalog of all published studies.
10.1. <sentence_start/>Multi-Marker Liquid Biopsy Models

Current multi-marker liquid biopsy models for MVI prediction are predominantly built on conventional circulating biomarkers, including tumor-related proteins such as AFP and PIVKA-II, as well as inflammatory mediators and other blood-derived indicators. <sentence_start/>Consistent with this approach, proteomic analysis of 50 HCC patients identified three plasma biomarkers, TALDO1, PDIA3, and PGK1, that were significantly upregulated in MVI-positive cases (FDR-adjusted <italic>p</italic> < 0.05). <sentence_start/>A machine learning model (PRIM) built on these markers demonstrated strong discriminatory performance, with AUC values ranging from 0.78 to 0.99 across three independent cohorts [<citation rid="B132-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhepr.2025.101481" pmid="40823177" pmcid="PMC12355497" count="1">132</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Given that PRIM was developed and validated across four independent medical centers with geographically distinct cohorts (Harbin, Changchun, and Shenyang), this model may be considered a validation candidate. <sentence_start/>However, all cohorts were retrospectively recruited within Chinese populations, and prospective evaluation in ethnically and geographically diverse settings is warranted before clinical application. <sentence_start/>Similarly, serum CXCL8, CXCL9 and CXCL13 were significantly elevated in MVI-positive HCC patients and positively correlated with Child-Pugh scores and AFP levels. <sentence_start/>The combined chemokine panel achieved robust MVI prediction, with an AUC of 0.86, sensitivity of 74.39% and specificity of 85.71% [<citation rid="B133-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2217/bmm-2023-0064" pmid="37218545" count="1">133</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This model should currently be regarded as an exploratory model, as validation was limited to an internal retrospective cohort without independent external confirmation.

Although multi-marker liquid biopsy models improve MVI prediction by integrating diverse circulating biomarkers, current models predominantly remain at the exploratory stage, relying on retrospective single-center cohorts with internal cross-validation [<citation rid="B133-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2217/bmm-2023-0064" pmid="37218545" count="1">133</citation>]; one model (PRIM) has advanced to validation-candidate status through multicenter external validation [<citation rid="B132-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhepr.2025.101481" pmid="40823177" pmcid="PMC12355497" count="1">132</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The ratio of candidate features to MVI-positive cases is often high, raising the risk of overfitting, whereby models capture dataset-specific noise rather than generalizable biological signals. <sentence_start/>Few studies report calibration metrics (e.g., calibration plots and Brier scores) or perform decision-curve analysis to quantify clinical net benefit across a range of risk thresholds [<citation rid="B134-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2021/9996358" pmid="34513751" pmcid="PMC8433031" count="1">134</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The optimal probability threshold for classifying patients as high-risk MVI versus low-risk MVI has not been standardized across studies, and the transportability of these models to different patient populations, including those with different HCC etiologies, geographic regions, and healthcare settings, remains untested. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, current models rely heavily on protein-based features, particularly high-throughput proteomics, which are costly, technically variable, and lack standardization, while the incremental predictive value of adding such complex biomarkers to simpler models based on routine clinical variables has rarely been formally quantified through net reclassification improvement (NRI) or integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) analyses [<citation rid="B135-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/sim.2929" pmid="17569110" count="1">135</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Emerging biomarkers such as ctDNA, ctRNA, and EVs may provide complementary information and further enhance diagnostic accuracy when integrated into existing models.
10.2. <sentence_start/>Liquid Biopsy-Clinicopathological Integration Models

Integrated models combining liquid biopsy biomarkers with clinicopathological features leverage established clinical variables to improve MVI risk stratification and inform individualized therapeutic clinical management [<citation rid="B57-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/liv.14463" pmid="32279416" pmcid="PMC7496978" count="1">57</citation>,<citation rid="B136-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gassur.2025.102245" pmid="41072847" count="1">136</citation>].

A representative model incorporating ctDNA allele frequency with tumor size achieved strong predictive performance, with an AUC of 0.92, sensitivity of 89.7% and specificity of 80.0% in the training cohort, and 78.6% sensitivity and 81.8% specificity in the validation cohort. <sentence_start/>In addition to diagnostic accuracy, this model also showed value in predicting recurrence-free survival [<citation rid="B57-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/liv.14463" pmid="32279416" pmcid="PMC7496978" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This model should currently be regarded as an exploratory model, as the training and validation cohorts were derived from a 2:1 random split of a single-center cohort (<italic>n</italic> = 73) without independent external validation. <sentence_start/>Similarly, nomogram-based models integrating clinicopathological factors, such as tumor diameter and HBV status, with serum biomarkers including AFP, AFP-L3%, PIVKA-II, and CA125 demonstrated stable performance, with AUCs of 0.806 and 0.818 in development and validation cohorts, respectively [<citation rid="B137-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/08941939.2025.2484539" pmid="40254744" count="1">137</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This model should currently be regarded as an exploratory model, as the development and validation cohorts were derived from a 3:1 random split of a single-center retrospective dataset (<italic>n</italic> = 1027), without independent external validation. <sentence_start/>Other models combining tumor differentiation, tumor size ≥ 5 cm, and blood-based markers such as PIVKA-II ≥ 90 mAU/mL and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio ≥150 achieved AUCs of 0.81 and 0.83 in training and validation sets, with good calibration and clinical net benefit [<citation rid="B136-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gassur.2025.102245" pmid="41072847" count="1">136</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This model should currently be regarded as an exploratory model, as the training and validation sets were derived from a 7:3 random split of a single-center retrospective cohort (<italic>n</italic> = 300) without independent external validation.
