Overall, these models combine the robustness of clinicopathological variables with the non-invasive advantages of liquid biopsy, improving preoperative MVI assessment. <sentence_start/>However, all currently published models in this category remain at the exploratory stage, having been developed and internally validated within single-center retrospective cohorts [<citation rid="B57-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/liv.14463" pmid="32279416" pmcid="PMC7496978" count="1">57</citation>,<citation rid="B136-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gassur.2025.102245" pmid="41072847" count="1">136</citation>,<citation rid="B137-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/08941939.2025.2484539" pmid="40254744" count="1">137</citation>]. <sentence_start/>While the integration of clinicopathological variables generally enhances model robustness compared with biomarker-only approaches, several important limitations persist. <sentence_start/>Most models are derived from surgical series with inherent selection bias, as patients deemed resectable represent a subset with more favorable tumor biology and preserved liver function, limiting generalizability to the broader HCC population [<citation rid="B138-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1245/s10434-021-10235-3" pmid="34235600" pmcid="PMC8591001" count="1">138</citation>]. <sentence_start/>External validation in geographically and etiologically distinct populations remains limited; a model developed in an HBV-endemic Asian cohort may not perform equivalently in a Western cohort with predominantly metabolic-associated HCC [<citation rid="B139-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cgh.2024.02.028" pmid="38484945" count="1">139</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Moreover, the incremental value of liquid biopsy features over established clinical predictors, including tumor size and AFP, has not been systematically quantified [<citation rid="B140-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12885-025-14268-9" pmid="40361115" pmcid="PMC12076900" count="1">140</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The stability of model features across studies is also low, with different combinations of biomarkers and clinicopathological variables emerging from different cohorts, suggesting that feature selection may be driven more by dataset-specific associations than by consistent biological signals. <sentence_start/>In addition, current models are often constrained by retrospective single-center designs, high costs, lack of standardization, and variability in selected model features. <sentence_start/>While ctDNA-based models have demonstrated clinical value, emerging biomarkers such as ctRNA and EVs may provide complementary biological information and further enhance predictive performance. <sentence_start/>Their integration with clinicopathological features may facilitate the development of more accurate, reproducible, and standardized models for preoperative MVI prediction.
10.3. <sentence_start/>Liquid Biopsy-Imaging Integration Models

Liquid biopsy integrated with imaging features combines molecular and morphological information, enabling accurate preoperative prediction of MVI in HCC and supporting imaging-guided clinical management [<citation rid="B141-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.aohep.2020.07.002" pmid="32768591" count="1">141</citation>,<citation rid="B142-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2024.1371432" pmid="39055557" pmcid="PMC11269143" count="1">142</citation>].

A representative scoring model incorporating CTCs ≥3/3.2 mL, AFP ≥158 ng/mL, and des-γ-carboxy prothrombin (DCP) ≥ 178 mAU/mL with imaging features such as tumor diameter ≥ 59 mm and unsmooth margins achieved strong performance, with an AUC of 0.922, sensitivity of 86.49%, and specificity of 90.20% [<citation rid="B141-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.aohep.2020.07.002" pmid="32768591" count="1">141</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This model should currently be regarded as an exploratory model, as the analysis was conducted on a single-center retrospective cohort (<italic>n</italic> = 227) without a dedicated validation cohort or external validation. <sentence_start/>Similarly, a nomogram combining AFP >800 ng/mL with MRI features, including arterial phase edge enhancement, incomplete capsule, and intratumoral vascular enhancement, showed stable efficacy, with AUCs of 0.871 and 0.878 in training and validation cohorts [<citation rid="B143-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.21037/qims-2025-758" pmid="41669472" pmcid="PMC12883496" count="1">143</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This model should currently be regarded as an exploratory model, as validation was limited to a 1:1 random split of a single-center retrospective cohort (<italic>n</italic> = 236), supplemented by 5-fold internal cross-validation, without independent external validation. <sentence_start/>Another radiogenomic nomogram integrating plasma miR-21 with MRI-derived tumor size and radiomic score also demonstrated high accuracy (AUC = 0.900, sensitivity = 0.970, specificity = 0.722) [<citation rid="B142-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2024.1371432" pmid="39055557" pmcid="PMC11269143" count="1">142</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This model should currently be regarded as an exploratory model, as the training (<italic>n</italic> = 116) and validation (<italic>n</italic> = 52) cohorts were derived from a single-institution retrospective dataset without independent external validation. <sentence_start/>Other predictive models based on gadobenate-enhanced MRI combined AFP with features such as peritumoral hypointensity and atypical enhancement patterns, yielding AUCs around 0.83 [<citation rid="B144-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2022.992301" pmid="36110937" pmcid="PMC9470230" count="1">144</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This model should currently be regarded as an exploratory model, as validation was performed using 4-fold internal cross-validation on a single-center retrospective cohort (<italic>n</italic> = 164) without independent external validation.

These models fully leverage the complementary strengths of liquid biopsy and imaging, enabling the non-invasive and reproducible assessment of MVI. <sentence_start/>However, all currently published imaging-liquid biopsy integration models remain at the exploratory stage, having been derived from single-center retrospective cohorts with internal validation only [<citation rid="B141-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.aohep.2020.07.002" pmid="32768591" count="1">141</citation>,<citation rid="B142-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2024.1371432" pmid="39055557" pmcid="PMC11269143" count="1">142</citation>,<citation rid="B143-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.21037/qims-2025-758" pmid="41669472" pmcid="PMC12883496" count="1">143</citation>,<citation rid="B144-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2022.992301" pmid="36110937" pmcid="PMC9470230" count="1">144</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Direct comparative data indicate that integrated models combining CTCs with imaging perform best in predicting MVI (AUC = 0.922), followed by ctDNA-clinicopathological models, while single-biomarker assays show the lowest predictive accuracy [<citation rid="B57-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/liv.14463" pmid="32279416" pmcid="PMC7496978" count="1">57</citation>,<citation rid="B133-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2217/bmm-2023-0064" pmid="37218545" count="1">133</citation>,<citation rid="B141-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.aohep.2020.07.002" pmid="32768591" count="1">141</citation>]; however, these comparisons are limited by the exploratory nature of the underlying studies, and relative rankings may not be reproducible in external validation settings. <sentence_start/>Notably, multi-omics integration represents a promising strategy for addressing the limitations of single-biomarker approaches, although its added value over simpler models must be demonstrated through prospective studies with predefined analysis plans. <sentence_start/>By combining imaging and liquid biopsy data, these models have the potential to improve preoperative MVI prediction and enable more individualized risk assessment. <sentence_start/>However, imaging-liquid biopsy integrated models also introduce additional methodological and practical complexity. <sentence_start/>Radiomics feature extraction remains non-standardized across CT and MRI platforms, reconstruction algorithms, and segmentation protocols, limiting reproducibility across institutions [<citation rid="B145-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1148/radiol.2020191145" pmid="32154773" pmcid="PMC7193906" count="1">145</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The relative contribution of imaging versus liquid biopsy features to overall model performance is rarely reported through formal feature-importance or ablation analyses, making it difficult to determine whether the increased cost and complexity of multimodal data collection are justified. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, many imaging features incorporated into these models, such as irregular tumor margins and peritumoral enhancement, are themselves established correlates of MVI, raising the question of whether liquid biopsy biomarkers provide independent predictive information beyond high-quality imaging [<citation rid="B146-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000513704" pmid="33981625" pmcid="PMC8077694" count="1">146</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although current models integrating CTCs, miRNAs, and serum markers have demonstrated clinical utility, emerging biomarkers such as ctDNA and EVs may offer complementary molecular information with higher biological resolution. <sentence_start/>Their incorporation into imaging-based frameworks may further refine multimodal characterization and improve predictive performance. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, prospective studies with pre-specified imaging acquisition protocols, standardized liquid biopsy collection time points, predefined analytical workflows, and blinded MVI endpoint adjudication are required to determine the true incremental value and clinical applicability of these integrated models [<citation rid="B147-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7326/M14-0698" pmid="25560730" count="1">147</citation>].
11. <sentence_start/>Therapeutic Strategies for MVI-Positive HCC Patients

It is important to note that liquid biopsy-based prediction of MVI has not yet been validated for treatment selection in routine clinical practice. <sentence_start/>Most studies discussed in this section stratified outcomes according to histopathologically confirmed postoperative MVI status rather than preoperative liquid biopsy-derived risk estimates. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the clinical implications outlined below should be viewed as a potential framework for future MVI-guided management, pending prospective validation, establishment of clinically actionable risk thresholds, and incorporation into consensus guidelines. <sentence_start/>Until such evidence becomes available, treatment decisions should continue to rely on established clinical, radiological and pathological criteria.

According to the Chinese Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Liver Cancer 2022 (CLCG 2022) [<citation rid="B148-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000530495" pmid="37901768" pmcid="PMC10601883" count="1">148</citation>], MVI is a key determinant of the biological heterogeneity and aggressiveness of HCC and is strongly associated with postoperative recurrence risk and long-term prognosis. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, routine assessment of MVI is recommended as part of postoperative pathological evaluation.

The principal translational value of liquid biopsy approaches lies in their potential to provide preoperative estimation of MVI risk. <sentence_start/>If validated in large prospective cohorts, these biomarkers could shift MVI assessment from the postoperative to the preoperative setting, enabling earlier risk stratification and providing complementary information for multidisciplinary treatment planning.

This section therefore summarizes current evidence regarding the incorporation of MVI status, or future MVI risk estimates, into surgical and perioperative management strategies for HCC. <sentence_start/>Particular emphasis is placed on surgical approach, resection margin strategy, liver transplantation, and perioperative locoregional therapies, with the goal of advancing risk-adapted and MVI-informed clinical decision-making.
11.1. <sentence_start/>Hepatectomy

Hepatectomy, the surgical removal of the liver portion containing the tumor, is the most widely used potentially curative treatment for early HCC patients with preserved liver function and no significant portal hypertension [<citation rid="B149-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhep.2018.08.027" pmid="30236834" count="1">149</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The type and extent of resection, including anatomical resection (AR), non-anatomical resection (NAR), and surgical margin width, exert a crucial influence on postoperative outcomes. <sentence_start/>This influence is mediated through their effects on the clearance of micrometastases and the preservation of the hepatic parenchyma. <sentence_start/>MVI is a significant predictor of recurrence and poor prognosis [<citation rid="B150-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1245/s10434-008-9846-9" pmid="18324443" count="1">150</citation>,<citation rid="B151-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0016-5085(94)90419-7" pmid="8194710" count="1">151</citation>], and it may influence the formulation of surgical strategies. <sentence_start/>For MVI-positive tumors, wider margins combined with AR may be beneficial, whereas for MVI-negative tumors, parenchyma-sparing NAR can achieve comparable outcomes. <sentence_start/>Preoperative MVI assessment is crucial for formulating surgical strategies, balancing tumor control with liver function preservation, and optimizing survival rates.
11.1.1. <sentence_start/>Surgical Margin Width Selection

In HCC, surgical margins are generally classified as narrow (≤0.5 cm) and wide (>1.0 cm). <sentence_start/>The 2022 CLCG guidelines recommend a personalized approach to surgical margins in cases of HCC with MVI, given its strong association with postoperative recurrence [<citation rid="B148-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000530495" pmid="37901768" pmcid="PMC10601883" count="1">148</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This approach is biologically motivated by evidence that MVI can extend beyond the macroscopic tumor boundary [<citation rid="B152-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00261-024-04463-w" pmid="39333413" count="1">152</citation>], raising concerns regarding residual microscopic lesions following resection.

Multiple studies have demonstrated that a wider margin (generally >0.5-1.0 cm) may remove peritumoral microscopic metastases, thereby reducing recurrence and improving survival [<citation rid="B153-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00268-020-05881-9" pmid="33386452" count="1">153</citation>,<citation rid="B154-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1245/s10434-011-2195-0" pmid="22203184" count="1">154</citation>,<citation rid="B155-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fmed.2020.00139" pmid="32478080" pmcid="PMC7232563" count="1">155</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, recent data suggest that when negative margins and high AR rates are achieved, long-term survival rates may not differ significantly across margin width categories (≤0.3 cm, 0.3-1.0 cm, >1.0 cm), regardless of MVI status [<citation rid="B156-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11605-020-04765-6" pmid="32779082" count="1">156</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This suggests that, at least in certain cases, outcomes in MVI-positive tumors, particularly larger ones, may be driven more strongly by the systemic or intrahepatic micrometastatic burden than solely by local surgical margin control.

Clinically, the practice of employing a wide margin is frequently constrained by background liver disease. <sentence_start/>In China, more than 80% of HCC patients have cirrhosis [<citation rid="B157-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11427-017-9259-9" pmid="29417360" count="1">157</citation>], and preservation of functional liver reserve often limits the feasibility of performing wide margins. <sentence_start/>In summary, although the survival benefit of wider resection margins remains controversial, current evidence suggests that MVI status may serve as an important modifying factor in surgical margin planning, helping to balance oncological benefit against preservation of hepatic functional reserve; however, integration of preoperative MVI risk prediction into routine surgical decision-making awaits further prospective validation.
11.1.2. <sentence_start/>Anatomical Resection (AR) and Non-Anatomical Resection (NAR)

AR and NAR are two fundamental surgical approaches for HCC. <sentence_start/>AR involves the resection of the tumor and the corresponding portal vein territory to eliminate potential portal vein spread, whereas NAR focuses on achieving tumor-free margins while preserving functional parenchyma, without regard for segmental anatomy [<citation rid="B158-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1055/s-2008-1040608" pmid="3022387" count="1">158</citation>,<citation rid="B159-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" pmid="2996162" count="1">159</citation>]. <sentence_start/>According to CLCG 2022, The choice between AR and NAR should be an individualized decision based on hepatic functional reserve and tumor biology [<citation rid="B148-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000530495" pmid="37901768" pmcid="PMC10601883" count="1">148</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this context, MVI status or the preoperative risk of MVI, serves as a critical factor in adjusting surgical strategy, favoring AR when liver function is adequate, while supporting the use of NAR in patients with limited liver reserve or those for whom liver parenchyma preservation is a priority.

Given that MVI reflects early vascular dissemination, AR is theoretically expected to confer a survival advantage in tumors. <sentence_start/>However, clinical evidence remains conflicting. <sentence_start/>AR offers limited survival benefit in patients without MVI or with well-differentiated tumors, suggesting its value may be greater in high-risk MVI patients [<citation rid="B160-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.surg.2013.10.009" pmid="24439747" count="1">160</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Other studies further indicate that AR combined with a wide margin (>1 cm) can synergistically improve outcomes in high-risk MVI patients [<citation rid="B161-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2217/fon-2019-0117" pmid="30968698" count="1">161</citation>,<citation rid="B162-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/JS9.0000000000000204" pmid="36917129" pmcid="PMC10389431" count="1">162</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, this benefit has not been consistently validated in the broader MVI cohort [<citation rid="B163-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jgh.13603" pmid="27671209" count="1">163</citation>,<citation rid="B164-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/ans.15396" pmid="31618805" count="1">164</citation>], and the effect may be constrained by factors such as tumor size or impaired liver function [<citation rid="B154-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1245/s10434-011-2195-0" pmid="22203184" count="1">154</citation>,<citation rid="B165-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.surg.2007.12.003" pmid="18374043" count="1">165</citation>]. <sentence_start/>By preserving parenchyma, NAR is often more suitable for cirrhotic patients, particularly those with limited hepatic reserve [<citation rid="B166-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00268-003-7308-x" pmid="15022021" count="1">166</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, in patients with MVI, NAR constitutes an independent risk factor for recurrence, as it may fail to eradicate micrometastases disseminating via tumor-associated portal vein branches. <sentence_start/>This risk is particularly pronounced when NAR is performed with narrow resection margins, as this approach is associated with the highest rate of early recurrence among all surgical methods [<citation rid="B162-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/JS9.0000000000000204" pmid="36917129" pmcid="PMC10389431" count="1">162</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, for MVI-positive patients with significant hepatic dysfunction, NAR may still be the only viable surgical option.

In summary, these findings indicate that MVI should be incorporated into clinical management as a stratification factor, rather than serving as an absolute determinant for selecting AR over NAR. <sentence_start/>Its pivotal role lies in refining patient stratification and supporting individualized surgical planning, particularly when balancing oncologic benefits against hepatic functional reserve. <sentence_start/>Notably, these considerations are based on histologically confirmed MVI following resection. <sentence_start/>The extent to which liquid biopsy-based preoperative MVI risk prediction can inform the AR-versus-NAR decision awaits dedicated prospective evaluation.
11.2. <sentence_start/>Liver Transplantation (LT)

Liver transplantation (LT) is considered the most definitive treatment for selected HCC patients, as it removes both tumors and diseased liver parenchyma [<citation rid="B167-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.14744/hf.2022.2022.0014" pmid="36177103" pmcid="PMC9510741" count="1">167</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Based on treatment sequence, LT can be classified into primary LT and salvage LT (SLT). <sentence_start/>Primary LT is performed as the first-line curative therapy, whereas SLT is reserved for tumor recurrence or liver failure following prior liver resection. <sentence_start/>In the context of limited donor organ availability, appropriate transplant candidate selection is essential to optimize post-transplant outcomes. <sentence_start/>MVI, a strong predictor of early recurrence and poor survival, has a significant impact on prognosis after both primary LT and SLT. <sentence_start/>Currently, transplant eligibility is largely determined by morphology-based criteria, including the Milan, UCSF, and Kyoto 5-5-500 frameworks [<citation rid="B168-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/lt.26003" pmid="33539659" count="1">168</citation>,<citation rid="B169-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/tri.13391" pmid="30556935" count="1">169</citation>,<citation rid="B170-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bjsopen/zrae079" pmid="39092977" pmcid="PMC11295212" count="1">170</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Incorporating MVI into these criteria may further refine risk stratification and inform optimal transplant strategy.
11.2.1. <sentence_start/>Impact of MVI on Primary Liver Transplantation Outcomes

MVI independently predicts poor outcomes after LT, being associated with higher recurrence and reduced survival [<citation rid="B171-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhep.2018.01.024" pmid="29410377" count="1">171</citation>,<citation rid="B172-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/SLA.0000000000003781" pmid="31972640" count="1">172</citation>,<citation rid="B173-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1470-2045(08)70284-5" pmid="19058754" count="1">173</citation>,<citation rid="B174-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.surg.2019.01.012" pmid="30878140" count="1">174</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, risk stratification studies have shown that the impact of MVI varies significantly among different patient subgroups. <sentence_start/>An East-West collaborative study reported that although living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) and liver resection (LR) can achieve comparable 5-year survival in early-stage HCC, MVI appears to exert a more detrimental impact on LDLT outcomes [<citation rid="B175-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhep.2014.01.022" pmid="24508550" count="1">175</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Other evidence suggests that selected low-risk MVI patients may still achieve favorable results after LT or AR [<citation rid="B176-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/gastro/goad035" pmid="37384119" pmcid="PMC10293589" count="1">176</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In very early tumors (<2 cm) [<citation rid="B177-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12664-017-0732-x" pmid="28194604" count="1">177</citation>] or in patients meeting the up-to-7 criteria [<citation rid="B178-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12072-011-9318-3" pmid="22016140" pmcid="PMC3360855" count="1">178</citation>], post-LT outcomes can remain acceptable despite MVI, underscoring the heterogeneity of its clinical effect.

Thus, MVI should not be regarded as an absolute contraindication to LT. <sentence_start/>Instead, it should be integrated into a multifactorial evaluation incorporating tumor burden, imaging characteristics, biological behavior, and liver function. <sentence_start/>More refined stratification models are still needed to identify which MVI-positive patients can derive meaningful benefit from LT while maintaining acceptable recurrence risk. <sentence_start/>Whether liquid biopsy-derived MVI risk stratification, as opposed to histologically confirmed MVI, can contribute meaningfully to LT candidate selection has not been studied and represents an important area for future investigation.
11.2.2. <sentence_start/>Impact of MVI on Salvage Liver Transplantation (SLT)

SLT offers a strategy to conserve donor livers by performing LR first and reserving transplantation for recurrence. <sentence_start/>Initial LR is feasible without compromising subsequent LT safety and can provide long-term survival if recurrence remains within transplant criteria [<citation rid="B179-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/hep.24680" pmid="21932387" count="1">179</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, MVI severely limits SLT efficacy [<citation rid="B175-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhep.2014.01.022" pmid="24508550" count="1">175</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Patients with MVI or satellite nodules frequently experience early and aggressive recurrence, progressing beyond transplant eligibility before SLT can be performed [<citation rid="B179-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/hep.24680" pmid="21932387" count="1">179</citation>,<citation rid="B180-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jhep.2024.06.018" pmid="38925272" count="1">180</citation>].To mitigate this limitation, the ab initio LT strategy proposes listing patients with high-risk pathology (MVI/satellites) immediately post-LR. <sentence_start/>Given early recurrence (<6 months) indicates aggressive biology, listing after ≥6-month observation is recommended. <sentence_start/>Preliminary data suggests this approach may improve survival in selected patients [<citation rid="B181-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/hep.28339" pmid="26567038" count="1">181</citation>].

In summary, SLT remains feasible for selected patients, but its utility is constrained by the rapid progression associated with MVI. <sentence_start/>Early incorporation of MVI status into post-resection surveillance may help identify patients who require closer monitoring, earlier transplant listing, or alternative strategies. <sentence_start/>Future studies should evaluate whether preoperative liquid biopsy-based MVI prediction can refine SLT candidate selection beyond histopathological criteria.
11.3. <sentence_start/>Transarterial Chemoembolization (TACE)

TACE is a widely used locoregional therapy for intermediate-stage HCC and remains the standard of care for patients who are unsuitable for curative treatments [<citation rid="B182-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/archsurg.133.2.183" pmid="9484732" count="1">182</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast, its role as a neoadjuvant approach in resectable HCC is limited, and current guidelines do not recommend routine preoperative TACE [<citation rid="B183-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/1097-0142(20010615)91:12<2378::AID-CNCR1271>3.0.CO;2-2" pmid="11413528" count="1">183</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although response to neoadjuvant TACE may provide insight into tumor biology and has been associated with prognosis, this response alone is insufficient for risk stratification. <sentence_start/>MVI consistently remains an independent adverse prognostic factor, underscoring the need for more refined, risk-adapted clinical management strategies [<citation rid="B184-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3892/ijo.2012.1711" pmid="23174998" count="1">184</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this context, attention has shifted toward the potential role of postoperative adjuvant TACE (PA-TACE) in improving outcomes after hepatectomy. <sentence_start/>Although PA-TACE has shown variable benefit overall [<citation rid="B185-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v21.i15.4627" pmid="25914472" pmcid="PMC4402310" count="1">185</citation>], substantial evidence demonstrates clear efficacy in high-risk subgroups characterized by factors such as large tumor size, multinodularity, macrovascular invasion, poor differentiation, or MVI [<citation rid="B186-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00432-009-0588-2" pmid="19408012" pmcid="PMC12160258" count="1">186</citation>,<citation rid="B187-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000007426" pmid="28816936" pmcid="PMC5571673" count="1">187</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Stratified analyses further reveal that PA-TACE improves survival and reduces early recurrence specifically in patients with high-risk MVI profiles, while offering limited benefit in low-risk populations [<citation rid="B188-diagnostics-16-02686" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejso.2025.110102" pmid="40300381" count="1">188</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Therefore, MVI serves as a key determinant for selecting patients who are most likely to benefit from PA-TACE after hepatectomy.

The presence of histologically confirmed MVI has been associated with differential benefit from adjuvant TACE in retrospective analyses, suggesting a potential role for MVI risk stratification in guiding perioperative TACE decisions. <sentence_start/>While response to neoadjuvant TACE may reflect tumor biology, evidence indicates that PA-TACE has been associated with survival and recurrence benefits in patients with high-risk MVI profiles in retrospective studies, supporting the concept of risk-adapted adjuvant therapy. <sentence_start/>Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and to determine whether preoperative liquid biopsy-based MVI prediction can identify patients most likely to benefit from adjuvant TACE.

Overall, current evidence highlights the important role of MVI in the clinical management of HCC. <sentence_start/>Histologically confirmed MVI is increasingly recognized as a marker of aggressive tumor biology and a higher risk of recurrence, and may contribute to risk stratification across different treatment settings. <sentence_start/>In surgical management, MVI status can be considered alongside other clinical and tumor-related factors when determining resection strategies and balancing oncological radicality against liver function preservation. <sentence_start/>In the context of transplantation, MVI may provide additional prognostic information that could help refine patient selection and post-resection listing strategies. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, MVI has been associated with differential responses to perioperative locoregional therapies and may help identify patients who are more likely to benefit from postoperative adjuvant TACE. <sentence_start/>However, these considerations are largely derived from studies using histologically confirmed MVI, and their applicability to preoperative MVI prediction models requires further prospective validation. <sentence_start/>Overall, incorporating MVI into a multidisciplinary and risk-adapted management framework may contribute to more individualized treatment planning and improved long-term outcomes in selected patients with HCC.
12. <sentence_start/>Translational Pathway Toward Clinical Implementation

The translation of liquid biopsy-based MVI prediction from research to clinical practice requires a structured, staged pathway. <sentence_start/>Stage 1 (Retrospective validation): Candidate biomarkers and models identified in discovery cohorts must undergo external validation in independent retrospective cohorts with histologically confirmed MVI to establish generalizability. <sentence_start/>Stage 2 (Prospective observational studies): Pre-specified biomarker panels, standardized collection and analysis protocols, and blinded MVI endpoint adjudication should be employed in prospective cohorts to evaluate real-world predictive performance and to establish optimal risk thresholds. <sentence_start/>Stage 3 (Clinical utility assessment): Studies must evaluate whether liquid biopsy-informed MVI risk stratification actually changes treatment decisions and, more importantly, improves patient outcomes. <sentence_start/>Ideally, randomized designs comparing liquid biopsy-informed management versus standard-of-care management should be conducted. <sentence_start/>Stage 4 (Threshold standardization): Predefined, validated risk thresholds must be established for each clinical decision context (surgical margin width, transplant eligibility, adjuvant therapy selection), as a single MVI-risk cutoff is unlikely to serve all clinical scenarios. <sentence_start/>Stage 5 (Guideline integration): Multidisciplinary consensus guidelines incorporating liquid biopsy-based MVI risk stratification should be developed through international collaboration before routine clinical implementation. <sentence_start/>This translational pathway, while demanding, provides a roadmap for the responsible and evidence-based integration of liquid biopsy into the preoperative management of HCC.
13. <sentence_start/>Discussion

MVI remains a pivotal determinant of early recurrence and long-term survival in HCC, yet its assessment continues to rely largely on postoperative histopathology and indirect imaging surrogates. <sentence_start/>As summarized in this narrative review, liquid biopsy offers a minimally invasive approach for preoperative MVI risk stratification by capturing tumor-derived molecular and cellular signals associated with vascular invasion and early dissemination. <sentence_start/>Current evidence indicates that ctDNA, CTCs, ctRNA and EVs provide complementary insights into distinct aspects of MVI-associated tumor biology, collectively supporting their potential role in improving preoperative risk assessment.

Accumulating evidence indicates that various liquid biopsy analyses reflect complementary aspects of MVI-associated tumor biology. <sentence_start/>ctDNA profiling, including somatic mutations, methylation profiles, and fragmentation features, enables the capture of genomic and epigenetic alterations associated with aggressive tumor behavior and early recurrence. <sentence_start/>CTCs, particularly mesenchymal and hybrid EMT phenotypes, provide direct cellular evidence of vascular intravasation and invasive potential, while quantitative CTC burden serves as a strong predictor of MVI. <sentence_start/>In parallel, ctRNA and EV-derived biomarkers expand the molecular landscape by reflecting invasion-associated regulatory programs and intercellular communication. <sentence_start/>Overall, these findings suggest that MVI may reflect a broader continuum of tumor invasion and dissemination, which can be partially captured by circulating biomarkers. <sentence_start/>However, current evidence primarily demonstrates associations rather than direct causality or relationships specific to MVI, and therefore should be interpreted cautiously. <sentence_start/>To facilitate an evidence-aware reading of the literature, we have systematically classified all reviewed biomarkers into four evidence tiers in Table 1, ranging from direct MVI histopathological validation (Level A) to mechanistic plausibility without clinical MVI data (Level D). <sentence_start/>This classification reveals that Level A evidence is concentrated in a relatively small subset of studies, primarily those evaluating ctDNA VAF, mSEPT9, CTC enumeration, M-CTC counts, serum miR-125b, circSETD3, S100P, and exosomal PRPSAP1. <sentence_start/>The majority of remaining biomarkers provide indirect (Level B-C) or purely mechanistic (Level D) evidence. <sentence_start/>This evidence imbalance represents a critical knowledge gap that should guide future prospective study design.

A key contribution of this review lies in its MVI-centric, integrative, and translation-oriented framework, which incorporates an explicit evidence-strength stratification to distinguish biomarkers with direct histopathological validation for MVI from those supported primarily by indirect clinical associations or mechanistic evidence. <sentence_start/>Unlike previous reviews that have primarily discussed liquid biopsy in HCC from diagnostic or prognostic viewpoints, this review examines ctDNA, CTCs, ctRNA, and EVs in relation to MVI as a unifying biological and clinical endpoint. <sentence_start/>Beyond integrating evidence across diverse biomarker categories and detection platforms, we further connect liquid biopsy findings with multi-omics predictive models. <sentence_start/>By combining complementary molecular signals within an evidence-graded framework, we aim to address the inherent limitations of single-biomarker approaches and provide a more rigorous assessment of MVI prediction. <sentence_start/>This integrative strategy highlights the potential of liquid biopsy-based multi-omics profiling for preoperative MVI evaluation, moving beyond isolated biomarker associations toward clinically actionable risk stratification.

Importantly, this review also highlights several limitations of the current evidence base. <sentence_start/>Most studies evaluating liquid biopsy biomarkers for MVI are retrospective, single-center investigations with substantial methodological heterogeneity in sample processing, analytical platforms and reporting criteria. <sentence_start/>Emerging multi-omics models have shown encouraging performance; however, their clinical translation is constrained by limited cohort sizes, a lack of external multicenter validation, undefined clinical cut-offs and the absence of standardized pre-analytical and analytical workflows. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, a notable knowledge gap is the absence of head-to-head comparative studies evaluating different liquid biopsy modalities-ctDNA, CTCs, ctRNA, and EVs-for MVI prediction within the same patient cohort. <sentence_start/>Without such comparative data, the relative clinical value and complementarity of each analyte class remain uncertain, and rational selection or prioritization of biomarkers for multi-analyte panels is precluded. <sentence_start/>Future studies should ideally collect and analyze multiple liquid biopsy fractions from the same blood draw in prospective cohorts with histologically confirmed MVI as the primary endpoint, enabling direct performance comparisons and assessment of additive predictive value.

Several limitations of this review should also be acknowledged. <sentence_start/>In addition, this review deliberately focused on four major liquid biopsy analyte classes that currently provide the most substantial evidence base for MVI assessment. <sentence_start/>Consequently, other emerging liquid biopsy approaches, including EV-derived metabolomic, proteomic, and other multi-omics signatures, were not systematically reviewed. <sentence_start/>Although these fields remain relatively underexplored in the context of MVI, they may provide additional biological insights and represent important directions for future investigation. <sentence_start/>As a narrative synthesis, it does not follow a formal systematic-review methodology and may therefore be subject to selection bias despite efforts to comprehensively evaluate the available literature. <sentence_start/>No quantitative meta-analysis was performed, precluding formal assessment of pooled diagnostic performance and between-study heterogeneity. <sentence_start/>In addition, publication bias may favor studies reporting positive associations, potentially inflating estimates of biomarker performance, while the rapid evolution of liquid biopsy technologies means that some recently developed high-sensitivity platforms and multi-analyte approaches may not be fully represented.

From a clinical perspective, liquid biopsy and its integration into multi-omics predictive models should not be regarded as a replacement for histopathology, but rather as a tool for biologically informed preoperative risk stratification. <sentence_start/>Identification of patients at high risk of MVI via validated multi-omics models may, following prospective clinical validation, support more precise risk-adapted management strategies. <sentence_start/>Importantly, the clinical utility and reliability of such models are likely to depend on the evidence strength of their constituent biomarkers, with models incorporating biomarkers directly validated against histopathological MVI expected to provide more robust clinical decision support than those based primarily on indirect or mechanistic associations. <sentence_start/>However, as outlined in the Translational Pathway, several stages of validation, including external cohort replication, prospective observational studies, clinical utility trials, and threshold standardization, must be completed before liquid biopsy-based MVI prediction can inform treatment selection, surgical planning, or transplant eligibility.

Looking ahead, progress in this field will necessitate large-scale, multicenter prospective studies, following the staged Translational Pathway, to validate liquid biopsy-based MVI signatures and multi-omics models, standardize end-to-end analytical pipelines through inter-laboratory harmonization, and define clinically actionable, context-specific risk thresholds. <sentence_start/>Integration of multi-analyte liquid biopsy data with standardized imaging features and clinicopathological variables will further enhance predictive accuracy, but must be accompanied by rigorous demonstration of incremental clinical value. <sentence_start/>By consolidating current evidence, bridging biomarkers with multi-omics models, and outlining a structured translational pathway, this review provides a framework for advancing the preoperative assessment of MVI in HCC and promoting individualized, risk-adapted clinical management.
